jamie.ops: Quick request — we need a concise runbook for operating spot/preemptible GPU capacity. Focus on drain procedures, interruption handling, and escalation paths. Can someone sketch a tight version we can paste into the runbooks page?

priya.eng: Yep. I can draft. Key things to cover: detection (cloud interruption notice/metadata), cordon+drain steps, autoscaler policy to kick up on-demand, pod priorities + PDBs, and an escalation checklist for SRE.

marco-sre: Add: mixed-capacity pools strategy (reserve % on-demand for critical SLOs), eviction handler for stateful jobs, and quick rollback to smaller models if GPU capacity drops. Keep commands ready.

jamie.ops: Nice. Let's keep it short (one-screen). Also include the exact kubectl commands we usually run and who to ping oncall for >5 node evictions.

priya.eng: Draft below — please copy into runbooks and tweak.

priya.eng: Runbook: Operating spot/preemptible GPU pools (short)
- Scope: spot/spot-like GPU node pools across cloud providers used for inference and batch training.
- Goals: minimize user-facing impact, keep critical latency SLOs, recover quickly, and control cost.

1) Detection
- Watch: cloud interruption APIs (AWS EC2 Spot interruption notices, GCP preemptible/spot metadata), node autoscaler logs, and node-ready/NotReady churn in cluster metrics.
- Alert rule (SRE): >3% node eviction rate in 5m or >2 GPU nodes evicted in 1m -> trigger paging.

2) Immediate actions (first 0-5 minutes)
- If auto-eviction detected but healthy: let autoscaler replace nodes.
- If large simultaneous evictions or pods failing: cordon and drain any remaining at-risk spot nodes to evacuate pods cleanly.

Commands (copy/paste):
```
# mark node unschedulable
kubectl cordon <node-name>
# drain gracefully, ignore daemonsets, allow with PDBs to respect disruption budgets
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
```
- Use --grace-period tuned per workload; for model servers 30-120s typical.
- If drain stalls due to a stuck pod: kubectl describe pod <pod> -> check for finalizers/volumes; if safe, delete pod with --force --grace-period=0 as last resort (coordinate with owners).

3) Autoscaler / capacity policies
- Ensure cluster autoscaler has mixed-mode enabled: prefer spot but allow on-demand nodes to replace to maintain SLOs.
- Keep a reserved on-demand cushion (recommended 10–25% of GPU capacity) for critical routes.
- Configure scale-up cooldowns low for on-demand pools so we can react quickly to large spot losses.

4) Workload classification / placement
- Critical inference pods: priorityClass=high, nodeSelector/affinity to on-demand pools or taint toleration for dedicated GPU on-demand.
- Best-effort batch/training: tolerate spot pool only, implement checkpointing and retries.
- Use PodDisruptionBudgets for any stateful parts and conservative minAvailable settings.

5) Eviction handling and graceful degradation
- Run eviction handler sidecar (checks metadata interruption messages) to gracefully flush caches, push state to S3, and deregister from load balancers.
- For model serving, implement fallback routes: ghost model or smaller quantized variant hosted on on-demand pool for minimal latency.

6) Escalation path (who to ping)
- Immediate: post to #eng-infra and @oncall-bot (auto-pager if threshold met).
- If >5 GPU nodes evicted or serving errors >5% for 10m: page SRE oncall (marco-sre) and Eng Platform lead (priya.eng).
- Exec/CS escalation: only if customer impact exceeds SLA or revenue-critical jobs fail — notify tina-prod and Head of Customer Success.

7) Post-incident tasks
- Collect logs: node events, kubelet logs, autoscaler decisions, cloud interruption messages.
- Run root-cause checklist: was it zone-level drain, quota, cloud preemption storm, or cluster misconfig?
- Update runbook with any config tweaks (e.g., increase on-demand cushion, change PDBs).

8) Best practices (short bullets)
- Tag spot pools with billing tags and monitor unit-cost per GPU-hour.
- Keep a small fleet of warm on-demand nodes in each region with GPU variants we use most.
- Prefer multi-zone distribution for spot pools to avoid zone-level mass preemptions.
- Automatically route low-priority workloads to cheaper regions where latency allows.

priya.eng: Implementation notes / snippets we use in infra repo:
- autoscaler config snippet (example):
```
nodeGroups:
  - name: gpu-spot
    minSize: 0
    maxSize: 200
    instanceTypes: [gpu-a100, gpu-a10]
    spot: true
  - name: gpu-ondemand
    minSize: 10   # reserve cushion
    maxSize: 100
    instanceTypes: [gpu-a100]
    spot: false
```

marco-sre: Add: during an active event, we prefer increasing on-demand pool size by a quick manual scale rather than waiting for slow autoscaler policies. Command: `gcloud compute instance-groups managed resize` or AWS equivalent. Document exact runbook command per cloud in the canonical page.

tina-prod: Also call out SLAs — if customer-facing latency degrades, switch traffic to fallback model and post a status update. Keep a short status template for #status page.

k8s-bot: Reminder: check PodDisruptionBudget violations with `kubectl get pdb` and list pods blocked by PDBs using `kubectl describe pdb <name>`.

priya.eng: OK I'll push this to https://redwood.internal/runbooks/spot-gpu and add the cloud-specific resize commands. Anyone want to add a one-line blurb about preferred cushion % per region?

marco-sre: For critical regions (us-west1, eu-west1) we run 15% on-demand cushion. Other regions 10%. Add as recommended defaults.

jamie.ops: Awesome — this is exactly what we needed. I'll copy into the runbook and land docs PR. Thanks all :clap:
